d: Sixty-four independent golf brands: founder- and family-owned labels with no parent company or outside investors, with where each is based and what it makes.

d: Thirty-seven golf brands built to be seen — maximal prints, painted headcovers and graphics that were never going to be subtle.

d: Forty-six golf brands where a person still makes the thing — wedges ground by hand, headcovers cut one at a time, course maps painted to order.

d: Six golf brands cut for the private-club end of the game — clothing and shoes that clear any dress code without looking like they tried.

d: Twenty-seven golf brands that dress for a muni rather than a member-guest — public-course culture, parking-lot beer and no dress code anxiety.

t: Post-Round Golf Clothing Brands
d: Thirty-six golf brands making clothes that do not announce themselves off the course — wearable at the bar, the airport and everywhere after eighteen.

t: Quiet Luxury Golf Brands — Understated
d: Twenty-one golf brands working in restraint — no visible branding, considered fabric and cuts that say nothing at all across a car park.

t: Range Practice Gear Brands
d: Nine golf brands built for the people who are at the range more than the first tee — grips, shafts, carts and the unglamorous end of the bag.

t: Limited Drop Golf Brands
d: Eighteen golf brands that release in small runs and do not restock — if you are waiting for it to come back, it is not coming back.

t: Heritage Golf Brands — The Long-Running Names
d: Seventeen golf and adjacent brands with real longevity behind them — companies whose archive is older than most of the Brand Index.

t: New Golf Brands — Recently Added

t: Tour-Proven Golf Brands — Played at the Top
